title: Growth docs
intro: Growth handles your website's tracking pixels, cookie consent, conversion events, your own analytics and site-wide SEO (robots.txt, verification tags, IndexNow, an SEO checklist and redirects), plus a notice bar. Your website's tokens are in the Portal: open the website, then Install and tokens. The browser token is public and goes into your pages; the server token is secret and stays on your server.
localhost: Testing on your own computer: the browser token also works on pages served from localhost, *.localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1], on any port, over http or https. Those pages write into your website's real database, so visits you make there are counted. There is no test mode.
script: Add the page script to the head of every page, before the other products' scripts, so it hears their shop events. It shows the consent banner and the notice bar, loads your tags once the visitor consents to their category, and records anonymous analytics. In a single-page app it follows the pages the app opens itself (history.pushState and the back and forward buttons, when the path or the query string changes; history.replaceState when the path changes): each is a page view, its address is checked for a site search (once while the path and the term stay the same), its not_found marker is read a second later, once the page is drawn, and the notice bar follows its hidden pages. Everything it does follows the features that are on; with none on, it does nothing.
consent: The consent banner asks for your consent categories (the list Consent categories in Settings, PUT /v1/lists/consent_categories): necessary, preferences, analytics, marketing and the sale or sharing of personal data to start with, and any of your own (at most 10), each with its name and description for visitors, how it asks (required: always on; opt_in: off until the visitor agrees; opt_out: on until the visitor says no, as US privacy laws such as the CCPA allow for the sale or sharing of personal data, and off for a browser that sends Global Privacy Control), the Google Consent Mode v2 signals it grants (ad_storage, ad_user_data, ad_personalization, analytics_storage, functionality_storage, personalization_storage, security_storage) and, with Custom scripts on, its own scripts. A signal is granted when every category that lists it is on, so turning off the sale or sharing category takes ad_user_data and ad_personalization away even with marketing on. Tags load once their signals are granted: Google Analytics needs analytics_storage; the Meta and TikTok pixels and Google Ads need ad_storage and ad_user_data; the Tag Manager container loads once an opt-in category is on (or the visitor chose and left one beyond the required ones on), and Consent Mode tells its tags the rest; a category's scripts load once it is on. The banner sits at the bottom or top of the page, in the middle as a dialog over it, or in the bottom left or right corner ('Banner position'). The visitor's choice is kept in their own browser (localStorage, asked again after 12 months or the months you set in 'Ask again after', and when you add a category) and never sent to us. Google Consent Mode v2 starts from the categories that are on before a choice. Using your own consent tool instead? Leave the banner off and pass the choice on with SSGrowth.consent.set({ <category key>: true or false, … }) (an opt-out category left out stays on); SSGrowth.consent.get() answers { categories, at } or null, and SSGrowth.consent.open() reopens the banner's choices, for example from a 'Do not sell or share my personal information' link. Tags wait for consent by default; with 'Tags wait for the visitor's consent' off (Settings → Tags and consent), every category is on until the visitor chooses (an opt-out one stays off with Global Privacy Control), and a choice the visitor makes is still followed. Laws in many places require consent before tracking: if you turn it off, you are responsible for following the law where you operate.
privacy: Analytics are anonymous: no IP address, user agent, cookie or cross-site id is ever stored. A page view keeps the path (never the query string), whether it starts a visit (the start time of the visit is kept in the visitor's sessionStorage, never an id), the referring site or campaign, a device class from the screen width and the country your host's request header gives (x-vercel-ip-country, cf-ipcountry, cloudfront-viewer-country or x-country-code; turn country off in Settings). With 'Count only after analytics consent' on (the default), nothing is recorded before the visitor consents to analytics. Your server may also send a visitor's events itself: POST /v1/collect with the server token and no Origin, naming the visitor's IP address in SS-Visitor-IP (used only for the per-visitor limit, never stored). The country then comes from the headers our host sets for your server's request, so it is your server's country, not the visitor's; turn country off if you send events this way. Want sessions? Set Detail to sessions (Settings → Visitor analytics): each visit in a browser tab then also gets a random session id, kept in that tab's sessionStorage (never a cookie or a cross-site id; it ends when the tab closes or after 30 minutes without a page view), the browser and system family (Chrome, Safari … and Android, iOS …; never the user agent) and, with country on, the city your host's header gives (x-vercel-ip-city, cf-ipcity or cloudfront-viewer-city). Nothing about a session is kept before consent when consent is required.
storage: Everything recorded goes into your own database (Connections → Database): raw events in ss_growth_analytics_events, removed by the database's expiry index after the retention you set (13 months by default; a change applies to events recorded afterwards), and daily totals in ss_growth_totals (one document per day: each batch the page script sends costs one insert of its events and one update of the day's totals, so a free database tier keeps up), kept forever. Days are the days of your business time zone (the time zone set in the Portal under Website settings, UTC without it): the daily totals, the analytics ranges (from and to) and the analytics dashboard all use it, and GET /v1/analytics answers it as timeZone. Days already counted keep their day when the time zone changes. GET /v1/events lists the raw events, newest first (type and session filter them); GET /v1/events/count and GET /v1/events/counts?by=type count them with the same filters. With the sessions detail, GET /v1/analytics also answers sessions (count, bounces, bounceRate in percent, averageDuration in seconds, pagesPerSession), browsers, systems, cities, vitalPages (each page's average Web Vitals, the slowest first), notFoundFrom (each missing page and where its visitors came from), live (visitors seen in the last 5 minutes and the page each last viewed, judged when you ask) and journeys (the 20 latest sessions of the range, each with its first 30 steps); GET /v1/events?session=<id> lists every event of one session. Each top list has 10 rows; ask for up to 100 with top.
events: Shop events are browser events on window. Ecommerce's shopper widgets send them; your own code may send them too. Growth records each one (Goals and funnels) and passes it to the pixels that are loaded, under the names of your conversion actions (Settings → the list Conversion actions, or PUT /v1/lists/conversion_actions: for each event its Meta, Google Analytics 4 and TikTok name, empty for not that pixel, and a Google Ads conversion label; to start with Meta ViewContent, AddToCart, InitiateCheckout, Purchase, Search and Contact, Google view_item, add_to_cart, begin_checkout, purchase, search and generate_lead, TikTok ViewContent, AddToCart, InitiateCheckout, CompletePayment, Search and Contact, and no Google Ads conversion until you give one its label; a Meta name that is not one of Meta's standard events is sent with trackCustom). Your own events: SSGrowth.track('book_demo', { plan: 'pro' }) (a name of lower-case letters, digits and _ from a letter; at most 10 properties, each a text, a number or true or false) is recorded when one of your goals or funnel steps names it (any other is dropped, so your database keeps only what you count) and goes to the pixels its conversion action names. A contact (ss:contact or SSGrowth.contact({ method })) is recorded too. Money is in minor units with its currency; pixels get major units. Items are named by their product id; with 'Item ids sent to the pixels' set to variant (Settings → Pixel events) they are named by their variant id, the product id when there is none. While your Tag Manager container is loaded, each event is also pushed to its dataLayer as a Google Analytics 4 event ({ event, ecommerce } for the shop events, after { ecommerce: null }), so the container's tags can take it. Is Google Analytics 4 set up inside your container? Turn on 'Google Analytics 4 runs inside Tag Manager' in Google tags: Growth then does not load Google Analytics itself and the container counts each event once.
page: Site searches are found on pages whose address has one of your search parameters (q, s, search, query by default; none when the setting is empty); SSGrowth.search(term, { results }) or the browser event ss:search ({ term, results }) records one from your code. Every site search also goes to the pixels that are loaded (Meta Search, Google Analytics search, TikTok Search; a search found in the page address only while 'Searches found in the page address go to the pixels' is on, the default), and so does a contact: SSGrowth.contact({ method }) or the browser event ss:contact ({ method }, for example whatsapp, phone or email) when a visitor taps your WhatsApp, phone or email link (Meta Contact, Google Analytics generate_lead, TikTok Contact). A page that does not exist is recorded when it carries the not_found marker or calls SSGrowth.notFound(). Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS, FCP, TTFB) are measured in the visitor's browser and sent together when the page is left, filed under the page the browser loaded (in a single-page app, the first page of the visit in that tab, as the browser measures them for the whole document). They are measured by web.dev's rules (as the web-vitals library does): CLS is the largest burst of layout shifts (shifts less than a second apart, at most 5 seconds; 0 for a page that did not shift), INP is about the 98th percentile of the page's interactions (the longest while there are fewer than 50), and LCP and FCP count only while the page was in view. With 'Also send them to Google Analytics 4' on, each one also goes to Google Analytics 4 (loaded by Growth or inside your Tag Manager container) as an event named after the vital, with value (milliseconds; CLS × 1000), metric_id (one id per vital and page load), metric_value, metric_rating, event_category (web-vitals), event_label (the metric id) and non_interaction. That works without Visitor analytics too: then the vitals go to Google Analytics only and nothing is kept in your database.
seo: robots.txt and the verification tags are served for your site to include: your server answers /robots.txt with what GET /v1/robots.txt gives (your rules plus a Sitemap line per sitemap) and adds the tags of GET /v1/verification to the page head. As Google advises for pages that need no indexing, robots.txt keeps crawlers out of them rather than letting them crawl and then drop each one: Disallow lines, added to each group of your rules (a User-agent: * group comes first when your rules have none), keep out addresses with a search parameter of Searches and 404s ('Keep search results out', on by default), addresses with a sort or filter parameter ('Sort and filter parameters to keep out'; attr.* covers every parameter starting with attr.) and private pages ('Private pages to keep out'; /cart keeps out /cart, /cart/… and /cart?…, never /cartoons). The last two are empty for every new website, whatever it is; a shop applies the online store preset in Settings in one click (sort, minPrice, maxPrice and inStock; /cart, /checkout and /account, as Ecommerce's storefront names them) and changes them to its own names. They never keep out / or a path holding your sitemap; never list a parameter or path of pages you want in search results (the SEO checklist fails a sitemap page or product image that robots.txt blocks). Search engines read them from your own domain. 'AI training crawlers to block' adds a group that keeps the crawlers you tick off the whole site (GPTBot, Google-Extended, CCBot, ClaudeBot, anthropic-ai, Applebot-Extended, Bytespider, meta-externalagent, cohere-training-data-crawler; none by default), and 'More crawlers to block' adds your own user agents (letters, digits, . _ and -, at most 30); search engines and AI answer bots that cite your pages still follow your own rules. Verification tags: Google, Bing, Meta and Yandex in the settings, and any other in the list More verification tags (PUT /v1/lists/verification_tags with { value: [{ name, content }] }, at most 20; paste the content or the whole tag; names that change how a page is shown or indexed, such as robots or viewport, are refused)
indexnow: IndexNow tells Bing, Yandex and the other search engines that take it about new or changed pages at once. Make your key with Generate in Settings (8–128 letters, digits or dashes; or type your own) and serve it as plain text at https://<your domain>/<key>.txt, or at the path you set as the key file address (for example /indexnow-key.txt); GET /v1/indexnow/key.txt gives it, and every submission names that address as the keyLocation. Submit addresses of your website with POST /v1/indexnow or the SEO checklist widget, when you ask; nothing is submitted by itself.
checklist: The SEO checklist reads your live website the way a search engine does, when you ask (the widget, or POST /v1/seo/checks from your server; never on a timer), and says for each check whether it passed, should be improved or must be fixed, what it found and how to fix it (widget texts, editable in Settings → Words and look → Widget texts), with a link to Google's Rich Results Test for each page, Google's own final check of rich results. One run reads robots.txt, the sitemap it names (else /sitemap.xml; of a sitemap index, its first 3 files), your pages (the home page, then the pages of its settings or the paths you send, at most 20), the old paths of up to 3 of your redirect rules and an address your site does not have: a removed product's when one is known (with Searches and 404s on, the most visited address of the last 90 days' 404 log at the level of a product page read, /products/* for /products/blue-lamp, that the sitemap does not list and no rule answers; a made-up address is read instead when it is a product page again), else a made-up one. Earlier product slugs that Ecommerce sends on to the new address are not tried: neither the sitemap nor your pages name them and Growth does not read Ecommerce's data, so add a redirect rule for an address you want checked. A full run (no paths sent) also picks sample pages from the sitemap: it reads up to 6 of its addresses (the first with images, the first with a query string, then the first of each group of addresses that share their first path segment) and keeps up to 4 of them of different kinds, a product first, then a collection page, then the rest in the sitemap's order (a filtered list, with a query string, counts as a kind of its own). A page's kind is its main schema.org type (Product, CollectionPage, Article, Event, DefinedTerm …; the home page is home): the product checks run on product types, the breadcrumb check on products and collections. Reads never follow a redirect and never run scripts, so the checks see the HTML your server sends, as a search engine first does; they go only to public https addresses, at most 4 at a time, each for at most 8 seconds and 2 MB (Google reads the first 2 MB of a page; a sitemap file up to 16 MB), and a run takes at most 25 seconds. With Web Vitals and Visitor analytics on, a run adds what your visitors measured in the last 28 days; with Searches and 404s on, the addresses of the last 90 days' 404 log that no redirect rule answers. The last full run is kept in your database (ss_growth_seo_reports, one document): GET /v1/seo/report answers it, the widget opens on it and checks again by itself when it is more than a day old, and a full run asked within 5 minutes of the last one answers that one (cached: true) without reading your site. A website runs it at most 10 times an hour. A finding you accept can be ignored: Ignore in the widget (seo.check; PUT /v1/admin/seo/ignored with { check, page, ignored }) or the list Ignored SEO findings (PUT /v1/lists/seo_ignored, entries { check, page }: page is a path pattern, * inside one segment and ** any, or empty for every page and the whole site); the report marks it ignored and counts it apart (summary.ignored), at once, also in a kept report. The title and description lengths are fixed (a good title is 10 to 60 characters, a good meta description 50 to 160). Each page read keeps what it gives search engines (pages[].head: title, meta description, canonical address, og:image, og:site_name), and its card shows it as a search result and a share card: the title and description measured by their width in pixels, so any language or script, against Google's usual widths (600 px and 920 px), with a warning where they may be cut.
redirects: Redirects send an old address of your website to its new page, for good (301 or 308; 308 keeps the request method, for forms) or for now (302 or 307, for a page that comes back, such as a seasonal sale: search engines keep the old address; 307 keeps the request method), or tell visitors and search engines that a page is gone for good (410). Google advises permanent redirects made by your server, kept for at least a year, each old address straight to its most relevant new page and never through a chain. Your server applies them: before it answers a request, it asks GET /v1/redirects/match?path= with the path and query string (204 when no rule answers it, else the code and the location to send), or edge middleware keeps the whole list from GET /v1/redirects/all and matches requests itself (example below). The list carries an ETag and Cache-Control: private, max-age=300: ask again at most every 5 minutes with If-None-Match and you get 304 while nothing changed, so a site on a free plan reads it rarely; changes reach it within 5 minutes, while /match answers at once (one read of your database each time, so you may ask only before answering a 404). A rule matches the path only: an exact rule its path, a prefix rule its path and every path under it, segment by segment (/blog matches /blog and /blog/news, not /blogger), and a prefix rule keeps the rest of the path (/blog → /news sends /blog/2019/a to /news/2019/a). A wildcard rule matches whole segments: * one segment and ** any number (/shop/*/item/* matches /shop/men/item/42), and its new page may name what they matched as $1 to $9 in order (/shop/*/item/* → /p/$2 sends /shop/men/item/42 to /p/42); a website has at most 100 wildcard rules. An exact rule wins, else the prefix or wildcard rule with the most fixed segments (a prefix rule's segments are all fixed; on a tie the wildcard rule; among wildcard rules the one with fewer **, then A to Z). Paths are compared normalized: one leading slash, repeated slashes as one, . and .. resolved, letters in one Unicode form (NFC: /café typed or encoded composed or decomposed is one path), characters outside URLs percent-encoded with upper-case hex, no trailing slash except for /, letter case kept (/Old and /old are two paths). A query string never takes part: a rule's old path with ? or # is refused, and the visitor's query string is passed on after the target's own (/old?utm_source=news → /new?ref=a&utm_source=news).
notice: The notice bar shows your announcements (Settings → the list Announcements, or PUT /v1/lists/announcements; at most 20), while 'Show the notice bar' is on (the default; turn it off to hide them all and keep them for later). Each has a key, its text, an optional link (an https address or a path on your website) and link text, when it shows (startsAt and endsAt as YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm on your business time zone's clock, the dashboard's date pickers; empty: at once and until you change it), the pages it shows on (empty: every page) and those it hides on (path patterns from /, where * is any characters inside one segment and ** any number of segments, for example /checkout/** or /sale-*), and whether visitors can close it and for how long: until they open another page (page), for the rest of their visit (visit) or for some days (days, dismissDays 1 to 365). A page shows the first announcement in your order that is on now, applies to it and is not closed (a changed text shows again). Place it with the notice_bar element, else it goes at the top of the page. Drawing your own bar? GET /v1/notice (browser token from your pages, or the server token from your server) answers { key, text, linkText, linkUrl, dismissible } of the announcement showing now, else null; add ?path=/the/page for that page's.
admin: Admin widgets run in your own admin with a ticket. The analytics dashboard (analytics.read) shows any range of days (chips for today, 7, 30 or 90 days, this month, last month and 12 months; any days from its More menu): visits per day, page views, revenue, ranked lists of pages, sources, devices and countries with See all, the funnel, searches and 404s, Web Vitals and the event log of every recorded event with a filter per type; with the sessions detail also live visitors, sessions, bounce rate, average time, pages per session, browsers, systems, cities, the slowest pages, where 404 visitors came from and the latest journeys, each with every event of the visit. With Conversion funnel on it also has a Products table: each product's views, add-to-carts, checkouts, purchases, units bought, revenue per currency, cart rate and conversion (purchases per 100 views), sorted by any column, with a CSV file of every product (GET /v1/analytics/products and /v1/analytics/products/csv for your server). It counts the shop events' items per product in the daily totals as they arrive (the raw events keep only ids and quantities, so storage stays light), with the name the events gave each product; Ecommerce's widgets send names and prices, and your own pages can too (items: [{ id, name, price, quantity }]). The SEO checklist (seo.check) opens on the last full check of your site and checks again by itself when it is more than a day old; it checks the pages of its settings and sample pages from your sitemap, or other pages you name, shows what passed, what to improve and what to fix with the reason and the steps, opens each page, tests it in Google's Rich Results Test, checks it again or submits it from its menu, and leads from the 404 log's check to the redirects widget on the same page; its IndexNow card (indexnow.submit) names your key file and submits pages. The redirects widget (redirects.edit) lists the rules, newest first, with a search and a filter by answer, adds, changes and deletes them, imports and exports CSV, and shows the suggestions from the 404 log, each opening a new rule. Include the script without data-token, place the widgets and register your ticket function. The widget calls it at start and 1 minute before the ticket expires; your server checks the user's sign-in and role every time. GET /v1/admin/events (with /count and /counts?by=type) is the event log's ticket route.
tickets: Your server asks for a ticket with the server token (never send the server token to a browser). The origin is the address of your admin page: any https origin, or a local one while testing. Tickets last 15 minutes and carry only the permissions of switched-on features.
api: Every route answers JSON except robots.txt and the IndexNow key, which answer plain text, and the redirects export, which answers CSV; POST /v1/collect answers 202 with how many events it kept, GET /v1/notice answers null while no notice shows, GET /v1/seo/report answers null until the SEO checklist ran in full, GET /v1/redirects/match answers 204 with no body when no rule answers the address, and GET /v1/redirects/all answers 304 while the list you keep is current. Errors are RFC 9457 problems with a stable code. Lists are paged with cursor and limit. Routes of a feature that is off answer 403 feature_off, and routes that read or write your database 403 database_not_connected until it is connected (Connections → Database). Below the route list, the reference gives every call with what it takes and answers.

import: Moving from another analytics system? Our admins switch Import on for the migration and off after it; ss-import sends the days with the server token only. POST /v1/import/totals takes NDJSON (Content-Type application/x-ndjson, at most 1,000 days or 4 MB per call; ?dryRun=1 checks and counts without writing), one day per line: { "day": "YYYY-MM-DD", "part": 0, "totals": { "<metric>": { "<key>": { "c": <count>, "s": <sum> } } } }, the day in your business time zone and the keys as readable text (Growth escapes them). Each metric must be one Growth counts (visits and page_views with the key "", page, source, device, country, funnel, revenue, search, vital and the rest), with keys of the form Growth writes, a whole count of 0 or more and a finite sum (only revenue, duration, vital_value and vital_page keep sums); unknown fields are refused by name, and the answer lists each refused line with what is wrong.

An imported day replaces that day's document in ss_growth_totals, so totals counted live that day before the import are replaced too; nothing is sent and no raw events are made. POST /v1/import/totals/prune with { "keep": [{ "day", "part" }, …] } removes imported days the source no longer has (days counted live are never removed); POST /v1/import/finish has nothing to derive; GET /v1/import/status answers the counts and the sums ss-import verify compares (days, visits, page_views). The analytics report reads imported days like any other.
seo_checklist: Checks of the whole site, each with its findings: robots_txt (ok, not_text: an HTML page in its place has no rules; missing, redirect, error: while robots.txt fails with a server error, Google stops crawling), robots_sitemap (ok, none), robots_blocks (ok, blocked: robots.txt keeps Googlebot from the home page, the sitemap or a page read, or Googlebot-Image from a product image, as Google reads its rules; a page of the checklist's own that the robots presets keep out on purpose, such as /cart, is not tried), sitemap (ok, missing, invalid, empty, too_large, file_missing), sitemap_urls (ok, bad: a sample address does not answer 200 itself; other_host), soft_404 (ok, moved: a removed product sends visitors permanently to another product page, its replacement; soft: the missing address answers 200; redirect: elsewhere, such as its category or the home page; error), redirects_live (ok, not_applied: an old path does not answer a redirect of its rule's kind, permanent 301 or 308 or temporary 302 or 307, to the rule's address, or 410 or 404 for a gone page; a wildcard rule is tried with each * and ** as the segment ss-growth-check), redirect_suggestions (none, some), verification (ok, none) and web_vitals_site (ok, needs_improvement, poor: Google wants LCP, INP and CLS good for at least 75% of visits; poor when more than a quarter of them are poor; judged from 5 measurements).

Checks of each page: reachable (ok, redirect: a failure for an address your sitemap lists; not_found, error, timeout, too_large, unreachable, not_read: the run's 25 seconds were up), noindex (ok, noindex, in_sitemap), title and description (ok, missing, short, long), h1 (ok, missing, several), canonical (ok, missing, several, relative, other_host, other_page, not_self: a page of your sitemap must name itself; invalid), lang, viewport, social, image_alt and image_size (ok, missing), structured_data (ok, none, invalid), on the home page site_data (ok, missing: Organization and WebSite), on product pages product_data (ok; incomplete: name, offers.price or offers.priceCurrency missing; partial: image or offers.availability missing), price_match (ok, not_shown: no price of the structured data is in the HTML your server sends) and server_html (ok, missing: the product's name is not in it), breadcrumbs on product, category and listing pages (ok, missing), response_time (ok up to 800 ms, slow up to 1,800 ms, very_slow), caching (ok: an ETag or Last-Modified header, with a Cache-Control that lets it be kept; none; no_store: Cache-Control no-store keeps nothing to ask again about) and, with the sessions detail, web_vitals (the average LCP, INP and CLS of the pages at the page's level, /products/* for /products/blue-lamp, over 28 days, from 5 measurements; ok, needs_improvement, poor).
redirects: Staff manage the rules in the redirects admin widget (permission redirects.edit), or your server does with the server token: at most 5,000 rules per website, one per old path. A rule's new page is a path on your website or an https address (an https address on your own domain is kept as its path). Every change is checked against all the rules: a loop (a request that comes back to an address it passed) or a chain (a request that would pass two rules, or end at a page a 410 rule removes) is refused, naming the addresses one request would pass; so is a deletion that would leave a chain behind. Every change is written to the activity log.

Suggestions: the pages visitors could not find most in the last 90 days (Searches and 404s records them) that no rule answers yet, each with a suggested new page when a page visitors did open has the same last segment (/old/blue-lamp → /lamps/blue-lamp). CSV: the export has the columns from, match, to, code and note; an import takes the same columns in any order (the Redirect from and Redirect to columns other platforms export also work), separated by commas, semicolons or tabs. A dry run (the default) lists what would change and every problem by line; the import then adds or changes rules and never deletes any, and a file with any problem imports nothing.

build.meta_pixel: Add the page script with your browser token (Install and tokens in the Portal) to the head of every page, before the other products' scripts, and paste your pixel ID in Settings. Ecommerce's widgets send the shop events by themselves; your own pages dispatch ss:view_item, ss:add_to_cart, ss:begin_checkout and ss:purchase on window ({ currency, value, items }, money in minor units). Using your own consent tool instead of the banner? Pass the visitor's choice on with SSGrowth.consent.set({ analytics, marketing }).
build.google_tags: Add the page script with your browser token (Install and tokens in the Portal) to the head of every page, before the other products' scripts, and set your Google Analytics 4, Google Ads or Tag Manager ids in Settings. Ecommerce's widgets send the shop events by themselves; your own pages dispatch ss:view_item, ss:add_to_cart, ss:begin_checkout and ss:purchase on window, and they reach Google Analytics 4, your Ads purchase conversion and the Tag Manager dataLayer. Using your own consent tool instead of the banner? Pass the visitor's choice on with SSGrowth.consent.set({ analytics, marketing }).
build.tiktok_pixel: Add the page script with your browser token (Install and tokens in the Portal) to the head of every page, before the other products' scripts, and paste your TikTok pixel ID in Settings. Ecommerce's widgets send the shop events by themselves; your own pages dispatch ss:view_item, ss:add_to_cart, ss:begin_checkout and ss:purchase on window ({ currency, value, items }, money in minor units). Using your own consent tool instead of the banner? Pass the visitor's choice on with SSGrowth.consent.set({ analytics, marketing }).
build.custom_scripts: Nothing on your pages beyond the page script with your browser token (Install and tokens in the Portal): paste your scripts in Settings as analytics or marketing scripts, and the page script adds them once the visitor consents to that category. Using your own consent tool instead of the banner? Pass the visitor's choice on with SSGrowth.consent.set({ analytics, marketing }).
build.consent_banner: Nothing to place: the page script with your browser token (Install and tokens in the Portal) shows the banner on every page, at the bottom or the top as set in Settings, where you also set after how many months a visitor's choice is asked again (12 by default, 1 to 24). The banner links to your privacy page, set once in the Portal under Website settings › Domains, pages and legal. Add a Cookie settings button, for example in your footer, that calls SSGrowth.consent.open(), so visitors can change their choice.
build.visitor_analytics: Add the page script with your browser token (Install and tokens in the Portal) to the head of every page; it records each page view, also the pages a single-page app opens itself. Connect your database (Connections → Database) and let its user create indexes. See the numbers in the analytics dashboard admin widget (analytics.read) in your admin, with tickets from your server, or read them from your server with GET /v1/analytics.
build.conversion_funnel: Your goals and funnels (Settings → Goals and Funnels, or PUT /v1/lists/goals and /v1/lists/funnels): a goal is an event (a shop event, contact, or your own event) or a page (a path pattern, * inside one segment and ** any number of segments); a funnel has 2 to 8 such steps in order (the shop funnel, view → cart → checkout → purchase, to start with; at most 30 goals and 10 funnels). The page script hears the shop events: Ecommerce's widgets send them by themselves; on your own pages, dispatch ss:view_item, ss:add_to_cart, ss:begin_checkout and ss:purchase on window with { currency, value, items: [{ id, price, quantity }] }, money in minor units, and orderId on a purchase; send your own with SSGrowth.track(name, props). Each goal and step is counted per day as it happens (a page pattern from when a goal or step names it): the analytics dashboard widget and GET /v1/analytics show each goal's count, each funnel's steps with the share of the step before, and the revenue per currency.
build.searches_404s: With the page script on every page, your search results page keeps the term in a search parameter of its address (q, s, search or query by default; yours in Settings), or your code calls SSGrowth.search(term, { results }). Your 404 page carries <meta name="ss-growth-page" content="not_found"> or calls SSGrowth.notFound().
build.web_vitals: Nothing beyond the page script with your browser token in the head of every page: it measures the vitals in the visitor's browser and sends them when the page is left. To have them in Google Analytics 4 too, turn on 'Also send them to Google Analytics 4' in Settings (it needs Google tags with Google Analytics 4).
build.robots_verification: Your server answers /robots.txt with the text of GET /v1/robots.txt and adds the tags of GET /v1/verification ({ tags: [{ name, content }], html }) to the head of your pages, both called with the server token, so search engines read them from your own domain. Set your rules, sitemaps and verification codes in Settings; without a sitemap set, robots.txt names https://<your domain>/sitemap.xml (where Ecommerce's sitemap route serves it). robots.txt keeps search results, sorted and filtered lists and private pages out of crawling by default: match them to your storefront's own names in Settings: the search parameters of Searches and 404s (q, s, search and query by default), Sort and filter parameters (sort, minPrice, maxPrice and inStock by default) and Private pages (/cart, /checkout and /account by default), and never list a parameter or path of pages you want in search results (products, categories, landing pages, page numbers, images).
build.indexnow: Make your key with Generate in Settings and serve it as plain text at https://<your domain>/<key>.txt, or at the key file address you set; your server gets it from GET /v1/indexnow/key.txt with the server token. Submit new or changed pages with POST /v1/indexnow { urls } from your server, or from the IndexNow card of the SEO checklist admin widget (indexnow.submit) in your admin, with tickets from your server.
build.seo_checklist: Nothing on your pages: the checklist reads your public pages, robots.txt and sitemap when you ask. To pass, your server sends each page's title, meta description, one canonical link, JSON-LD and main content (a product's name and price) in its HTML, answers 404 or 410 for addresses it does not have and applies your redirect rules. Set the pages to check in Settings and run it from the SEO checklist admin widget (seo.check) in your admin, with tickets from your server, or with POST /v1/seo/checks from your server; GET /v1/seo/report gives the last full run.
build.redirects: Your server or edge middleware applies the rules before it answers a request: keep the list from GET /v1/redirects/all and ask again at most every 5 minutes with its ETag in If-None-Match (304 while nothing changed), or ask GET /v1/redirects/match?path= for one address (204 when no rule answers it), for example only before answering a 404; both with the server token. Staff manage the rules in the redirects admin widget (redirects.edit) in your admin, with tickets from your server.
build.notice_bar:
Nothing beyond the page script with your browser token: the bar appears at the top of the page, or where you place
. Set the text, the link, the dates and the pages it hides on in Settings. Drawing your own bar instead? Read GET /v1/notice?path= with the browser token from your pages, or with the server token from your server.
build.import: Nothing on your website: for your migration, our admins switch Import on, run ss-import, which sends your past daily totals to POST /v1/import/totals with the server token, and switch Import off after it.
